screens.title: Animation Events & Scripting Integration
screens.subtitle: Synchronize animation frames with gameplay code and control animation state from C#

narration.text: Animation Events connect the visual timing of an animation clip to your game logic. In practice, an Animation Event is a marker on a clip that calls a public method on a component attached to the same GameObject as the Animator exactly when that frame is played. This is how you make footsteps play when a foot hits the ground, spawn particle effects at a precise impact frame, or register damage at the moment a weapon connects. You will also learn how to control Animator parameters from code, using SetFloat, SetBool, SetInteger and SetTrigger to drive blend trees and state transitions based on input or game state. Throughout this lesson you will see concrete examples: adding events in the Inspector, writing the public handler methods that receive optional parameters, and combining animation events with checks such as collision or raycast fallbacks so your game logic remains robust if an event is misconfigured. By the end you will understand the practical tradeoffs of relying on events versus physics checks and how to design safe, maintainable animation-driven interactions.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Animation Events call public methods at specific frames; scripts and Animator parameter control let gameplay and animation remain synchronized and robust.

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide hands-on work with Animation Events and scripting. First, you will understand the purpose of Animation Events: why markers exist and how they map to public C# methods on the same GameObject. Second, you will learn how to add and configure events inside an animation clip, including how to position markers precisely and supply optional parameters like a string or a float. Third, you will practice writing public methods that the events call, with safe checks for components such as an AudioSource so handlers do not fail at runtime. Finally, you will learn how to control Animator parameters from code and query animator state to make well-timed decisions. Each objective pairs a concrete skill with why it matters — for example, syncing footsteps preserves immersion, while safety checks prevent crashes. As you progress, use the verified competency milestone to confirm you can add events, implement handlers, and control animation from code reliably in Play mode.

screens.title: What is an Animation Event?
screens.subtitle: A timeline marker that calls a public method at runtime

narration.text: An Animation Event is a single, precise mechanism: a marker placed on an animation clip's timeline that invokes a public method on a component that lives on the same GameObject as the Animator at runtime. The marker holds a Function name and optionally one parameter: Float, Int, String, or Object. The practical effect is tight synchronization — you can make sound effects, particle spawns, and gameplay logic happen exactly when the animation shows it. For example, adding an event at a footfall frame and calling a method like PlayFootstepSound ensures audio plays when the foot contacts the ground. A subtle gotcha is scope: the method must be public and the function name spelled exactly as the method name, otherwise Unity logs a warning and the call is skipped. Another nuance is clip ownership: events belong to the clip itself, so if the same clip is used on multiple layers or characters, the event will call methods on each GameObject's relevant component. This makes events powerful for reusable clips, but also requires consistent component placement. Think of Animation Events as precise, frame-accurate signals; pair them with runtime checks such as null checks or collision tests to ensure your gameplay remains robust if an event is missed or misconfigured.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: An Animation Event is a clip-level marker that calls a public method on the same GameObject when the animation reaches that frame.

content.html:
Definition

Animation Event

A frame-precise marker inside an animation clip that calls a public method on a component attached to the same GameObject as the Animator.

Why it matters
  • Sync audio and VFX exactly to animation timing.
  • Trigger gameplay logic at the visually correct moment.
  • Keep animation-driven behavior reusable across characters.
Common misconception

Events are not global; they call methods only on the same GameObject as the Animator and require public methods with matching signatures.

Example: Footstep
Add an event at each footfall frame and set the Function to PlayFootstep or PlayFootstepSound. The named method will be invoked at those frames to play an AudioClip via an AudioSource component.
Concrete example

If PlayFootstep is called by the event, ensure the method is public and that an AudioSource exists so the handler can call PlayOneShot without errors.

Example call
PlayFootstep() → plays a footstep sound when a foot hits the ground.
Parameter note
Events can pass a String like "LeftFoot" so one handler can choose which sound to play.
Key Takeaway

Use Animation Events for frame-accurate triggers, but add runtime checks so your game is robust if the event fails.

screens.title: Add and Configure Animation Events
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: place a marker, assign Function, and apply changes

narration.text: Adding an Animation Event is a simple, repeatable workflow in the Animation Inspector. First, select the animation clip in the Project window and open it in the Inspector's preview area. Move the timeline scrubber to the exact frame where you want the event to occur, then click Add Event to place a marker. Drag the marker slightly to fine tune timing. With the marker selected, the Inspector reveals the event settings: set the Function name to match the public method you will write, and, optionally, choose and enter a parameter — Float, Int, String, or Object. After configuring each event, click Apply on the clip so the changes persist. A common pitfall is forgetting to Apply, which leaves events unsaved. Another common error is misspelling the function name; Unity will warn in the Console and the call will be skipped. If you are adding multiple events for similar frames, use consistent naming and parameters so the same handler can process them. For clips reused across characters, confirm each character has the necessary component with the public method, or the event will be ignored at runtime. This process gives precise control over timing while keeping the clip portable when used carefully.

keyIdea.title: Add events safely
keyIdea.text: Place a marker at the target frame, assign a Function name, optionally pass a parameter, then click Apply to save the clip changes.

content.html:
Workflow
  1. Select clip. Open the animation in the Inspector preview to reach the timeline.
  2. Place marker. Move the scrubber to the target frame and click Add Event.
  3. Configure. Set Function name and optional parameter type and value.
  4. Apply. Click Apply on the clip so the event is saved with the asset.
Pitfalls
  • Misspelling the Function name causes a warning and no call.
  • Forgetting to Apply leaves temporary events that won't persist.
  • Events belong to the clip; reused clips will call the same Function for each GameObject using them.
Visual checklist
Marker placed
Ensure the marker sits exactly on the intended frame.
Function set
Function name must match a public method on the GameObject.
Parameter checked
If you pass a parameter, the method signature must accept the matching type.
Apply clip
Click Apply to make the event persistent on the asset.
Pro tip

Use clear Function names like PlayFootstep or TriggerAttackDamage so many events are easy to read in the Inspector.

screens.title: Write Event Handler Methods
screens.subtitle: Public methods, component checks, and safe runtime behavior

narration.text: Handler methods called by Animation Events must be public and match the expected signature for any passed parameter. A robust pattern is to cache references in Start, check for nulls, and provide safe fallbacks. For example, a PlayFootstep method can check for an assigned AudioSource and an AudioClip before calling PlayOneShot. For attack logic, TriggerAttackDamage might play a whoosh sound then perform a short-range overlap or raycast to find enemies rather than trusting the event alone. The chapter supplies example scripts that show this pattern: get the Animator and an AudioSource with GetComponent in Start, log an error if the Animator is missing, and create public void methods for events. A good handler keeps effect logic compact and delegates complex systems such as applying damage to dedicated managers. Remember that Unity will log a warning if it cannot find the method, so clear Console messages and null checks make debugging faster. These practices keep events stable and safe when clips are reused or modified. Write Event Handler Methods means make public handler methods, cache components in start, check for nulls, and prefer short, testable responsibilities in event handlers.. In practical terms, public methods, component checks, and safe runtime behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Handler pattern
keyIdea.text: Make public handler methods, cache components in Start, check for nulls, and prefer short, testable responsibilities in event handlers.

content.html:
Example script
<!-- Escaped C# code block --> 
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerAnimationEventHandler : MonoBehaviour
{
  public AudioSource audioSource;
  public AudioClip footstepClip;
  public AudioClip attackWhooshClip;

  void Start()
  {
    if (audioSource == null)
    {
      audioSource = GetComponent<AudioSource>();
      if (audioSource == null)
      {
        audioSource = gameObject.AddComponent<AudioSource>();
      }
    }
  }

  // Called by Animation Event for footsteps
  public void PlayFootstep()
  {
    if (footstepClip != null && audioSource != null)
    {
      audioSource.PlayOneShot(footstepClip);
      Debug.Log("Footstep event triggered!");
    }
  }

  // Called by Animation Event for attack damage/effect
  public void TriggerAttackDamage()
  {
    if (attackWhooshClip != null && audioSource != null)
    {
      audioSource.PlayOneShot(attackWhooshClip);
    }
    Debug.Log("Attack damage event triggered!");
    // Example safe fallback: short raycast to confirm a hit
    RaycastHit hit;
    if (Physics.Raycast(transform.position + Vector3.up * 1f, transform.forward, out hit, 1.5f))
    {
      Debug.Log("Attack hit: " + hit.collider.name);
    }
  }
}
Walkthrough
  • Start() caches or creates required components so events can rely on them.
  • PlayFootstep() checks clip and audio source before playing to avoid null references.
  • TriggerAttackDamage() shows a fallback raycast so damage logic does not rely solely on the event.
Pro tip

Keep event handlers small: trigger systems or managers rather than embedding full damage logic directly inside the event method.

screens.title: Passing Parameters from an Event
screens.subtitle: Use Float, Int, String or Object to add context to a handler

narration.text: Animation Events can pass a single optional parameter to the method they call. The available types are Float, Int, String, and Object. This is very useful when the same animation clip needs to handle slightly different behaviors without duplicating clips. For instance, a walk clip could pass the string "LeftFoot" or "RightFoot" so a single PlayFootstep(string foot) method chooses the correct audio. An attack event might pass an Int damage value to a TriggerAttackDamage(int amount) handler. If you pass an Object, the event will try to reference an asset such as a GameObject or a ScriptableObject — be careful because those references must be resolved at edit time. The method signature must match the chosen parameter type exactly: Unity uses the event type to select the proper overload. A common mistake is changing a method signature after adding events — this can break the call. Test parameterized events in Play mode with debug logs and ensure you update both the clip and the script consistently so the event payload and handler align. Passing Parameters from an Event means use float, int, string, or object to provide context to a handler; the method signature must match the chosen type exactly.. In practical terms, use float, int, string or object to add context to a handler. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Parameter types
Float: Pass continuous values like intensity or volume.
Int: Pass discrete numbers such as damage amount.
String: Pass identifiers like "LeftFoot" to reuse handlers.
Object: Reference an asset or GameObject for advanced behaviors.
Signature requirement
The method must accept exactly the type you configured. If no parameter is used, define a parameterless public void method.
Examples
String example

Use the string to select left or right foot sound.
Int example

Pass damage so a single handler can apply variable damage values.
Watch out

Changing a method signature after placing events can break calls. Keep scripts and clips in sync.

screens.title: Control Animator Parameters from C#
screens.subtitle: SetFloat, SetBool, SetInteger, SetTrigger — driving animation from gameplay

narration.text: Controlling the Animator from code is how game state and player input influence visuals. The primary A P I methods are animator. SetBool, SetFloat, SetInteger and SetTrigger. Use SetFloat for continuous values like speed that feed Blend Trees and produce smooth transitions. SetBool suits states such as IsJumping, SetInteger can select discrete animation variants, and SetTrigger is ideal for one-off transitions like a jump or attack animation. Acquire the Animator reference in Start using GetComponent and store it for repeated use. In Update you might read Input. GetAxis or your movement velocity and call animator. SetFloat("MoveSpeed", Mathf. Abs(verticalInput)) to update a Blend Tree. Use SetTrigger("JumpTrigger") when handling a jump input to start a one-off animation. Querying state with GetCurrentAnimatorStateInfo helps you avoid conflicting actions: check IsName("AttackState") before allowing another attack. These APIs give a clean separation: scripts determine intent, Animator blends the visual result. Keep parameter names consistent and case-sensitive between code and the Animator Controller to avoid silent mismatches. Control Animator Parameters from C# means use setfloat, setbool, setinteger and settrigger to update animator parameters from gameplay code and keep parameter names consistent with the controller.. In practical terms, setfloat, setbool, setinteger, settrigger — driving animation from gameplay. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Animator API
keyIdea.text: Use SetFloat, SetBool, SetInteger and SetTrigger to update Animator parameters from gameplay code and keep parameter names consistent with the Controller.

content.html:
Key methods
animator.SetFloat("Parameter", value) — continuous values for Blend Trees.
animator.SetBool("Parameter", value) — binary states like IsGrounded.
animator.SetInteger("Parameter", value) — discrete selection indices.
animator.SetTrigger("Parameter") — fire a one-time transition event.
Example use
float vertical = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");
animator.SetFloat("MoveSpeed", Mathf.Abs(vertical));
if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump")) animator.SetTrigger("JumpTrigger");
Best practices
  • Cache the Animator reference in Start for performance.
  • Match parameter names exactly between code and the Animator Controller.
  • Use GetCurrentAnimatorStateInfo to gate actions while another animation is active.
Key Takeaway

Animator parameter methods let code express intent while the Animator system handles blending and transitions; keep the boundary clean and explicit.

screens.title: Querying Animator State & normalizedTime
screens.subtitle: Check current state and progress to make timing decisions

narration.text: When you need logic that depends on the animation's progress, query the Animator's state. GetCurrentAnimatorStateInfo(layerIndex) returns an AnimatorStateInfo structure with helpful properties. Use IsName("StateName") to confirm which state is active, which is useful to prevent actions such as triggering a second attack while the first is still playing. Use normalizedTime to understand how far the current state has progressed: it is 0 at start, 1 at end for a single-play state, and increases beyond 1 for looping states. For example, you can allow a combo attack only after normalizedTime exceeds 0.7 so input is accepted at the correct animation moment. These queries are especially helpful with transitions and layer blending where simple flags are not sufficient. Remember that reading state info is a snapshot; check it in Update or during the event handler to make immediate decisions. Also acknowledge that relying solely on normalizedTime can be brittle if your Animator Controller has complex transitions — test with the actual controller and adjust thresholds accordingly. Querying Animator State & normalizedTime means use getcurrentanimatorstateinfo to query the active state and normalizedtime to check progress, enabling guarded actions and combo windows.. In practical terms, check current state and progress to make timing decisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: AnimatorStateInfo
keyIdea.text: Use GetCurrentAnimatorStateInfo to query the active state and normalizedTime to check progress, enabling guarded actions and combo windows.

content.html:
State queries
IsName("AttackState") — check whether a specific state is playing on the base layer.
normalizedTime — returns progress; use thresholds to time follow-up actions or combos.
Example
var info = animator.GetCurrentAnimatorStateInfo(0);
if (info.IsName("AttackState") && info.normalizedTime > 0.7f)
{
  // allow combo
}
Guidance
  • Use normalizedTime thresholds, not exact values, to tolerate small timing variations.
  • Test thresholds with transitions and blends enabled in your Animator Controller.
  • Combine state checks with event handlers for redundancy when dealing with critical gameplay logic.
Pro tip

Use state checks to prevent input spam or conflicting animations, and validate normalizedTime values in Play mode for your specific controller.

screens.title: Events vs Physics Checks
screens.subtitle: When to rely on Animation Events and when to use collision or raycasts

narration.text: Animation Events are ideal for frame-accurate effects like footstep sounds or visual timing where the animation is the source of truth. However, for gameplay-critical actions such as applying damage, it's safer to combine events with physics checks. Relying only on events can fail if the component is missing, the method name is misspelled, or the event is not applied. A hybrid approach uses the event to play a sound or trigger a visual, while the actual damage application either double-checks with a weapon collider or performs a short raycast at the same moment. This redundancy prevents missed hits and improves reliability across networking or complex controllers. Consider also that physics checks account for actual spatial relationships — an event that triggers damage based only on timing may hit a target that is visually missed due to latency or animation blending. Use events for timing and cosmetics, and physics or overlap checks for authoritative gameplay results. This clear separation reduces bugs and makes replication across characters easier to reason about. Events vs Physics Checks means use animation events for timing and visuals; pair them with physics or collision checks when applying authoritative gameplay effects.. In practical terms, when to rely on animation events and when to use collision or raycasts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hybrid approach
keyIdea.text: Use Animation Events for timing and visuals; pair them with physics or collision checks when applying authoritative gameplay effects.

content.html:
Events
Pros: frame-accurate, easy for sound/VFX, clip-level reuse.
Cons: dependent on correct Function names and GameObject components; can be skipped if misconfigured.
Physics checks
Pros: spatially authoritative, works with colliders and networking, less fragile.
Cons: may need extra setup, less tied to precise animation frame without synchronization.
Use case: Footsteps
Events are perfect — cosmetic audio tied to frame timing.
Use case: Melee damage
Event can mark the moment, but confirm with a short raycast or collider overlap before applying damage.
Best practice
Design events for visuals and use physics for authoritative outcomes.

screens.title: Hands-on: Footstep and Attack Events
screens.subtitle: Step through setup, script, assign events, and test in Play mode

narration.text: This activity ties everything together. Start with a character that has a Walk and Attack animation. Add or confirm an AudioSource on the same GameObject. Create a script like PlayerAnimationEventHandler and expose public AudioClip fields for footsteps and attack whoosh. In Start, get or add an AudioSource so the handler can always play audio. In the Walk clip, add two events at the left and right footfall frames, and set Function to PlayFootstep or PlayFootstep with a String parameter like "LeftFoot". In the Attack clip, place an event at the swing peak and set Function to TriggerAttackDamage. Apply the changes to each clip. Enter Play mode and run the character. When the walk plays, you should hear footsteps and see Console logs. When the attack triggers, you should hear the whoosh and see the damage log; if you included a raycast fallback, verify hits only occur when an enemy is in range. Use this activity to validate your null checks, verify parameter passing, and practice matching Function names and signatures. After testing, reflect on whether the event was cosmetic or authoritative and whether a physics fallback is needed for reliability.
